questions.prompt: A SQL Server DBA new to Oracle assumes Oracle's SGA is 'just the buffer pool with a different name.' What specifically is wrong with that assumption, per Lesson 3?
options: The SGA is a single shared memory region made up of several distinct named components (buffer cache, shared pool, redo log buffer) that don't map one-to-one onto SQL Server's buffer pool
The SGA is always smaller in total size than SQL Server's buffer pool
The SGA only exists in Oracle RAC configurations, not in a single-instance Oracle database
The term SGA was removed starting with Oracle Database 19c
questions.explain: Oracle's System Global Area is a specific, named, multi-component shared memory structure — buffer cache, shared pool, redo log buffer, and more — each with its own job and sizing parameters. SQL Server's buffer pool is one shared memory space that also absorbs responsibilities Oracle deliberately splits out into the separate, private-per-process PGA. Assuming a one-to-one mapping produces a wrong mental model, not just wrong terminology.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about why organizations end up running multiple database platforms, per Lesson 2.
options: A merger or acquisition inherits whatever database platform the acquired company was already running
A legacy application built decades ago on one platform may keep running on that platform long after the company's current standard has changed
Licensing cost pressure can push companies to migrate some workloads toward open-source platforms like PostgreSQL or MySQL
A company running more than one database platform is, by definition, suffering from poor IT governance
Full standardization onto a single platform is usually quick and low-risk once a company decides to pursue it
questions.explain: Lesson 2 names mergers/acquisitions, legacy applications outliving a company's current standard, deliberate best-tool-for-the-job choices, and licensing cost pressure as the real, concrete reasons companies end up multi-platform. It explicitly pushes back on treating this as a sign of dysfunction, and explains that migrations are expensive and risky — the opposite of quick and low-risk — which is exactly why full standardization rarely actually happens.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: unlike MySQL and PostgreSQL, whose images are freely available on Docker Hub, the Oracle Database Free image is distributed through ________, which requires a free account and accepting a license agreement before you can pull it.
questions.explain: Oracle's licensing model keeps its database images off the public Docker Hub. Oracle Database Free is distributed through Oracle Container Registry (container-registry.oracle.com), which gates access behind a free account and a click-through license agreement — the same account/license gate a real job would require before installing Oracle software.

questions.prompt: A SQL Server DBA claims 'an Oracle instance is just what Oracle calls a database.' Which fact from Lesson 6 most directly disproves that claim?
options: Oracle RAC lets multiple separate instances, running on different servers, mount and open the exact same single database at the same time
Oracle instances run only on Linux, while Oracle databases can run on Windows
An Oracle instance has a default tablespace, while a database does not
Oracle databases are backed up with RMAN, while instances are backed up with Data Pump
SQL*Plus connects to the instance, while SQL Developer connects to the database
DBCA installs the Oracle software, while the Oracle Universal Installer creates the database
questions.explain: An instance (background processes plus SGA memory) and a database (datafiles, control files, redo logs on disk) are two separate things connected by a mount, not one combined unit. RAC proves this isn't just terminology: it lets multiple distinct instances on different physical servers mount and open one single shared database concurrently — something that only makes sense if instance and database are genuinely different things.
questions.distractorExplain: Option F reverses the two tools' actual jobs: the Oracle Universal Installer (OUI) installs the Oracle software into an Oracle Home, and the Database Configuration Assistant (DBCA) is what actually creates a database afterward. Getting the tools backwards doesn't disprove the instance/database claim at all — it's a separate mix-up about tooling, not about what an instance versus a database actually is.

questions.prompt: A row is inserted into a table. Per Lesson 10's storage hierarchy, which sequence correctly describes where that row physically lives, from smallest to largest unit?
options: Block, inside an extent, inside a datafile, inside a tablespace
Tablespace, inside a datafile, inside an extent, inside a block
Datafile, inside a block, inside an extent, inside a tablespace
Extent, inside a tablespace, inside a block, inside a datafile
questions.explain: Oracle's storage hierarchy runs tablespace (logical) down to datafile (the physical file backing it) down to extent (a contiguous group of blocks allocated as a segment grows) down to block (the smallest unit of I/O). Read from smallest to largest, a row lives in a block, inside an extent, inside a datafile, inside a tablespace.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the Oracle background process responsible for writing modified ('dirty') buffers from the buffer cache out to the datafiles on disk is ________.
questions.explain: DBWn (Database Writer) writes dirty buffers from the buffer cache out to the datafiles on disk. There can be more than one of these processes (DBW0, DBW1, ...) on systems with heavy write load, distinct from LGWR, which handles the redo log buffer instead.

questions.prompt: Match each Oracle tool to what it actually is, per Lesson 11.
right: Oracle's original command-line client, the closest thing to sqlcmd
Free Java-based GUI IDE for schema browsing and SQL/PL-SQL development
Lightweight web console bundled with the database for single-database monitoring
Separately-installed enterprise product for monitoring many databases across an organization
questions.explain: SQL*Plus is Oracle's original, scriptable command-line client. SQL Developer is the free GUI IDE closer to day-to-day development work. EM Express is the lightweight console bundled with one database for basic monitoring. Enterprise Manager Cloud Control is the full, separately-installed product for monitoring and managing many databases across an organization.

questions.prompt: A DBA grants the CONNECT role to a new user, assuming it still provides broad object-creation privileges the way it did in very old Oracle versions. What does CONNECT actually grant on a modern Oracle database, per Lesson 13?
options: Essentially just CREATE SESSION — enough to log in, nothing more
Full DBA privileges across the database
CREATE TABLE and CREATE PROCEDURE, scoped to the grantee's own schema
SELECT on every table in every schema
questions.explain: Since Oracle 10g, the predefined CONNECT role has been reduced to essentially just CREATE SESSION. Lesson 13 specifically warns against assuming it grants more than that on a modern database — object-creation privileges in your own schema come from RESOURCE, not CONNECT.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Oracle profiles, per Lesson 14.
options: Password-related limits in a profile, like FAILED_LOGIN_ATTEMPTS, are enforced by default with no extra switch needed
Resource limits like SESSIONS_PER_USER are silently ignored database-wide until ALTER SYSTEM SET RESOURCE_LIMIT = TRUE is run
Every Oracle user is assigned exactly one profile, defaulting to DEFAULT if none is specified at creation
Setting PASSWORD_REUSE_TIME alone, without also setting PASSWORD_REUSE_MAX, is enough to make Oracle enforce password reuse checking
IDLE_TIME is measured in seconds, not minutes
questions.explain: Password limits are always-on by default, while resource limits need RESOURCE_LIMIT flipped to TRUE at the instance level before they're enforced at all. Every user gets exactly one profile, DEFAULT unless another is assigned. Reuse checking specifically requires both PASSWORD_REUSE_TIME and PASSWORD_REUSE_MAX to be set — one alone does nothing. CONNECT_TIME and IDLE_TIME are both measured in minutes, not seconds.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of setting up and using a Virtual Private Database (VPD) row-filtering policy, per Lesson 15, in the correct order.
items: Write a PL/SQL policy function that returns the WHERE predicate to enforce
Register the policy with DBMS_RLS.ADD_POLICY, naming the schema, object, and policy function
An application sets a session context value, such as a region ID, before running its queries
Oracle transparently rewrites every matching query to add the policy function's predicate before it executes
questions.explain: A VPD policy needs a PL/SQL function defined first, since that function is what DBMS_RLS.ADD_POLICY registers against a schema and object. Once the policy is active, an application sets a session context value before querying, and Oracle then silently rewrites every matching statement to add that predicate — the application never has to remember to filter manually.

questions.prompt: One team needs to move just the HR schema into a different, empty Oracle database on another platform. A separate team needs to restore the entire production database to an exact point in time, mid-transaction, after a bad batch job. Which statement correctly matches each requirement to the right tool, per Lesson 17?
options: Data Pump for the schema move, since it exports portable logical objects; RMAN for the point-in-time restore, since it supports restore plus redo-based recovery
RMAN for the schema move, since it exports portable logical objects; Data Pump for the point-in-time restore, since it applies redo
Data Pump handles both jobs, since it can also apply redo for point-in-time recovery
RMAN handles both jobs, since it can selectively export just one schema's rows
Flashback Database handles the schema move; Data Pump handles the point-in-time restore
RMAN handles the schema move only if the destination platform runs the identical Oracle version; otherwise GoldenGate handles both jobs
questions.explain: Data Pump reads data through the engine and exports it as a portable logical description of objects and rows — exactly what's needed to move one schema onto a different platform or version. RMAN performs block-level physical backup and recovery, including applying redo to reach an exact point in time — exactly what's needed to undo a bad batch job across the whole database. Each tool does the job the other structurally cannot.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B swaps the two tools' actual jobs. RMAN backs up and restores physical datafiles block by block and has no concept of exporting just one schema's objects into a different, unrelated database. Data Pump has no redo-based recovery at all, so it cannot restore to an exact mid-transaction point in time — that capability belongs entirely to RMAN's restore-plus-recover model.

questions.prompt: A team takes a level 0 RMAN backup every Sunday and needs any restore during the week to require applying at most two backup sets total — the level 0 plus one more — no matter which day something goes wrong. Which nightly incremental strategy, per Lesson 19, achieves that?
options: Level 1 cumulative backups every night
Level 1 differential backups every night
A fresh level 0 backup every night instead of incrementals
Block change tracking alone, with no incremental backups at all
questions.explain: A cumulative level 1 backup captures every block changed since the most recent level 0, regardless of any level 1s taken since — so a restore only ever needs the level 0 plus the single most recent cumulative. A differential level 1 only captures changes since the most recent level 0 or level 1, whichever is more recent, which can require applying several differential backups in sequence by Friday.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Oracle's Flashback Database requires enabling flashback logging in advance and needs a dedicated storage area called the ________ to hold the flashback logs.
questions.explain: Unlike Flashback Query and Flashback Table, which rely on undo that's already present by default, Flashback Database requires setup in advance: flashback logging must be turned on, and the database needs a Fast Recovery Area to hold the flashback logs it depends on.

questions.prompt: Match each Flashback variant to what it actually does, per Lesson 21.
right: Reads data as it existed at a past moment via undo, with no advance setup required
Reverts a table's current rows to a past point in time, in place
Recovers an accidentally dropped table from the recycle bin
Rewinds the entire database using flashback logs, requiring advance setup
questions.explain: Flashback Query reads historical data through undo with zero advance configuration. Flashback Table actually reverts a table's rows in place. Flashback Drop recovers a dropped table from the recycle bin — a completely different mechanism. Flashback Database rewinds the whole database using flashback logs, but only works if flashback logging and a Fast Recovery Area were configured beforehand.

questions.prompt: Why did Oracle move away from chasing the buffer cache hit ratio as the primary tuning methodology, in favor of DB Time and wait events, per Lesson 23?
options: Hit ratio is an indirect proxy, while DB Time and wait events show directly, with evidence, where time is actually being spent
The buffer cache hit ratio was removed from Oracle entirely starting in 10g and no longer exists anywhere
Wait events only exist in RAC configurations, so single-instance databases had no choice but to switch methodologies
DB Time is easier to compute than a hit ratio, since it doesn't require querying any views at all
questions.explain: Chasing a hit ratio toward 99%+ is an indirect proxy for performance. DB Time and named wait events (db file sequential read, log file sync, and so on) let a DBA ask directly, with evidence, where time is actually going — a fundamentally more reliable starting point for the measure-identify-change-verify loop.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Oracle optimizer statistics, per Lesson 25.
options: Stale statistics can cause the Cost-Based Optimizer to choose a fundamentally wrong plan, not just a slower one
DBMS_STATS is the modern, supported way to gather optimizer statistics; ANALYZE TABLE is legacy for this purpose
A nightly automatic statistics-gathering job exists by default and refreshes tables with significant data changes
The automatic nightly stats job makes gathering statistics manually after a large one-time load unnecessary
A histogram is only useful for numeric columns, never for text columns like STATUS
questions.explain: Wrong statistics can make the optimizer choose a nested loop for what's actually a million-row input, not just a slower plan. DBMS_STATS is the supported tool; ANALYZE TABLE for optimizer statistics is legacy. A default nightly job refreshes statistics for tables with meaningful data changes, but Lesson 25 explicitly says that job isn't a substitute for gathering statistics deliberately right after a large one-time load. Histograms specifically help skewed columns regardless of data type — the lesson's own example is a text STATUS column that's 95% one value.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a bitmap index is the right choice for a ________-cardinality column — one with only a handful of distinct values across many rows — while a B-tree index suits columns with many distinct values.
questions.explain: Bitmap indexes store a bitmap per distinct value, which is efficient specifically when there are only a handful of distinct values (low cardinality) across many rows, like GENDER or ORDER_STATUS. A B-tree index, Oracle's default, suits high-cardinality columns with many distinct values instead.

questions.prompt: Why is describing Oracle RAC as 'Oracle's version of a SQL Server Failover Cluster Instance' inaccurate, per Lesson 30?
options: An FCI is active-passive (one node runs the instance at a time), while RAC is active-active (every instance processes transactions concurrently, all the time)
RAC doesn't use shared storage, while an FCI does
An FCI can scale out capacity by adding nodes, while RAC cannot
RAC requires Windows Server Failover Clustering underneath it, while an FCI does not
questions.explain: An FCI runs the instance on exactly one node at a time, with other nodes idle until a failover. RAC is genuinely active-active: every instance in the cluster processes transactions against the shared database concurrently, all the time, which is also what lets RAC deliver both scalability and availability together — not just a failover target.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Oracle Data Guard, per Lessons 28 and 29.
options: Maximum Protection mode will shut the primary down rather than risk committing data that no standby has confirmed receiving
A physical standby is kept current through Redo Apply, which is really continuous media recovery
A logical standby is open read-write for its own supplementary objects while still being kept current via SQL Apply
A switchover and a failover both always result in some amount of data loss
A logical standby remains physically identical to the primary after conversion, the same as a physical standby
questions.explain: Maximum Protection is the strictest mode: if no standby can confirm synchronous receipt, the primary actually shuts down rather than risk data loss. A physical standby stays current via Redo Apply, which is continuous media recovery. A logical standby is kept current via SQL Apply while remaining open read-write for its own extra objects. A switchover is a planned, no-data-loss role swap — only a failover carries potential data loss. And a logical standby is explicitly logically, not physically, identical to the primary once converted, unlike a physical standby.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of an in-place Oracle version upgrade, per Lesson 32, in the correct order.
items: Run the Pre-Upgrade Information Tool against the source database to flag version-specific blockers
Fix the flagged issues, such as invalid objects or deprecated features still in use
Run DBUA or AutoUpgrade to perform the in-place upgrade
Verify the upgraded database is healthy and functioning correctly on the new version
questions.explain: Lesson 32 treats the Pre-Upgrade Information Tool as mandatory, not optional, specifically so blockers are found while there's still time to plan around them. Only after flagged issues are fixed does DBUA or AutoUpgrade actually perform the in-place upgrade, and the course's recurring discipline — check first, change deliberately, verify after — means confirming the result's health is the last step, not something skipped once the upgrade tool finishes.

questions.prompt: An `orders` table takes dozens of concurrent inserts per second from checkout traffic. Under MyISAM's table-level locking versus InnoDB's row-level locking, what actually happens differently during that traffic?
options: Under MyISAM, every insert must wait for the entire table to be free, serializing all checkout writes against each other; under InnoDB, concurrent inserts touching different rows don't block each other at all
Both engines handle this identically, because table-level and row-level locking only differ for SELECT statements, not INSERT
InnoDB actually locks the whole table too, but recovers faster afterward, which is the only real difference under write load
MyISAM only locks the specific row being inserted, so there's no practical difference from InnoDB under this workload
questions.explain: MyISAM's table-level lock means every writer queues behind every other writer regardless of which row each one touches, visibly degrading under concurrent write load; InnoDB's row-level locking lets inserts to different rows proceed in parallel, which is exactly why InnoDB is the default for any table that gets real concurrent writes.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: because MySQL's storage engine is a per-table choice, running ________ lists every storage engine compiled into the running server and shows which one is the default.
questions.explain: SHOW ENGINES; enumerates every storage engine available on the running server and marks the default — the per-server inventory check that matters precisely because engine choice in MySQL is made per table, not per server.

questions.prompt: Match each MySQL tool or utility to what it's actually used for.
right: CLI utility for checking, repairing, and optimizing tables, mainly relevant to MyISAM
Runs a single SQL statement non-interactively and exits, used by health checks and monitoring scripts
Official GUI with a SQL editor, schema browser, ER diagram tool, and Performance Dashboard
CLI utility for quick administrative commands like status checks and pings
questions.explain: The -e flag runs one statement and exits, which is what health checks and scripts lean on. MySQL Workbench is the official GUI with a SQL editor, schema browser, ER diagrams, and a Performance Dashboard. mysqladmin handles quick administrative commands like status and ping. mysqlcheck checks, repairs, and optimizes tables, mostly relevant to MyISAM since InnoDB rarely needs it.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of running `mysql_secure_installation` on a fresh MySQL install, per the chapter, in the order the script actually performs them.
items: Optionally validate password strength policy
Set the root password
Remove anonymous user accounts
Disallow remote root login
Remove the test database
Reload privilege tables
questions.explain: This is the exact checklist order mysql_secure_installation runs: optionally install the password-validation policy, set the root password, remove anonymous accounts, restrict root to localhost, drop the test database, then reload the privilege tables so every change takes effect immediately.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about MySQL's `user@host` account model, per the chapter.
options: 'app_svc'@'10.0.4.%' and 'app_svc'@'localhost' are two genuinely separate accounts, even though they share a username
When multiple user@host patterns could match an incoming connection, MySQL authenticates against the most specific matching pattern, not just the first one found
'localhost' is just shorthand for '127.0.0.1', so the two host patterns behave identically on every platform
A bare username like 'analyst' with no host component is a valid, addressable MySQL account on its own
DROP USER 'analyst'@'192.168.1.%' removes only that exact user@host pair, leaving a differently-scoped account with the same username untouched
questions.explain: Two accounts sharing a username but differing by host are genuinely separate accounts. MySQL resolves an incoming connection against the most specific matching user@host pattern available, not just the first match. 'localhost' is treated specially — routed over the Unix socket where the platform supports it — not simply equivalent to '127.0.0.1'. A bare username with no host isn't a valid, addressable account on its own. And DROP USER removes only the exact pair named, leaving any other host-scoped account with the same username untouched.

questions.prompt: What does creating a MySQL account with `CREATE USER 'analyst'@'192.168.1.%' IDENTIFIED BY 'ChangeMe#2024';` actually grant that account the ability to do?
options: Authenticate to the server from a matching host — nothing else, since authentication and authorization are fully separate steps in MySQL
Authenticate and immediately run SELECT against every database on the server
Authenticate and run SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE against its own default database only
Authenticate, with full administrative privileges equivalent to root, since every new account inherits GRANT OPTION by default
Nothing at all — CREATE USER alone fails unless at least one GRANT statement is included in the same transaction
Authenticate and automatically see schema metadata for every database, but query no actual table data
questions.explain: CREATE USER only creates the account and sets how it authenticates. A freshly created MySQL account can log in and do essentially nothing until privileges are explicitly granted with GRANT — authentication and authorization are two fully separate steps in MySQL.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B is the closest-sounding wrong answer because it's tempting to assume login implies at least some read access somewhere, but MySQL grants zero privileges automatically on account creation — not even SELECT on one database — until a separate GRANT statement explicitly adds it.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: granting a role to a user with GRANT doesn't make it active automatically on connection. ________ 'app_readonly' TO 'analyst_jane'@'10.0.5.%'; is the statement that makes a granted role active automatically on every future connection for that user.
questions.explain: SET DEFAULT ROLE is what makes a granted-but-not-activated role active automatically on every future connection; without it, the user would need to run SET ROLE manually in each session before the role's privileges apply.

questions.prompt: This command is run against a live, busy InnoDB server. What does `--single-transaction` actually buy here?
options: A consistent MVCC snapshot of the data as of the moment the dump starts, taken without locking any tables, so read/write traffic continues normally
A guarantee that every table is locked for the entire dump, which is the only way to ensure consistency
A faster dump, since it skips exporting indexes and foreign keys entirely
Automatic compression of the SQL output so the resulting file is smaller
questions.explain: --single-transaction starts the whole dump inside one consistent InnoDB snapshot transaction, so every table is captured as of the same point in time without taking table locks — read/write traffic against the database keeps running normally during the backup.

questions.prompt: A full backup was taken at 2 AM and a damaging UPDATE ran at 9:15 AM. Put these point-in-time recovery steps in the correct order to recover to just before the damaging statement.
items: Restore the most recent full backup (from mysqldump or XtraBackup)
Identify which binlog files, and what position or timestamp within them, cover the gap since the backup
Run mysqlbinlog with a stop point set to just before the damaging UPDATE
Pipe the extracted binlog events into the mysql client to replay them against the restored database
questions.explain: Point-in-time recovery always starts from a full backup, then rolls forward: restore the backup, find which binlog files and position cover the gap since that backup, extract events up to (but not including) the damaging statement with mysqlbinlog, and replay them against the restored database to land one moment before the incident.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Percona XtraBackup compared to mysqldump, per the chapter.
options: XtraBackup performs a hot physical backup of InnoDB without stopping the server or taking blocking locks for most of its runtime
A backup directory must be --prepare'd, replaying the captured redo log, before it can be reliably restored with --copy-back
Restoring an XtraBackup backup means replaying SQL statements against a running server, the same as restoring a mysqldump
MySQL ships XtraBackup as a built-in utility alongside mysqldump, maintained directly by Oracle
XtraBackup supports incremental backups that capture only pages changed since a prior backup
questions.explain: XtraBackup is Percona's free, open-source hot physical backup tool, copying InnoDB's files while the server keeps running. An unprepared backup is unreliable to restore — --prepare replays the captured redo log to make the copied files consistent first. Restoring means putting prepared files back in place and starting the server, not replaying SQL, which is exactly how it differs from mysqldump. It also supports incrementals, keeping backup windows short on large databases. It is a third-party tool Percona built to fill a real gap, not something MySQL ships built-in or that Oracle maintains.

questions.prompt: An EXPLAIN on a slow query shows `type: ALL`, `key: NULL`, `rows: 480000`, `Extra: Using where`. What does this combination actually tell you?
options: MySQL is doing a full table scan of roughly 480,000 rows because no usable index exists for this query's filter, applying the WHERE condition after fetching every row
MySQL found a covering index and is reading the data entirely from that index without touching the table
MySQL needs to build a temporary table to complete a GROUP BY, which is unrelated to indexing
The query is already optimally indexed, and Extra: Using where simply confirms a WHERE clause exists in the SQL text
questions.explain: type: ALL means a full table scan, key: NULL means no index was used at all, rows: 480000 is the optimizer's estimate of how many rows it expects to examine, and Using where means the filter is applied after rows are fetched rather than narrowing the scan via an index — together this is the signature of a missing or unusable index on a table of meaningful size.

questions.prompt: Match each MySQL EXPLAIN output signal to what it actually means.
right: A full table scan — every row in the table is examined
No index was chosen for this table, even if one exists
MySQL needs an extra pass to sort the result set because no index could produce rows in the required order
The query is satisfied entirely from the index itself, without reading the underlying table rows
questions.explain: type: ALL flags a full table scan. key: NULL means no index was used for that table, which is a strong warning sign on a table you expected to be indexed. Using filesort means MySQL needed an extra sorting pass unaided by an index. Using index is the good sign — a covering index satisfies the query without touching table rows at all.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: InnoDB caches table and index data in memory to avoid disk reads, and the size of that cache is controlled by ________, typically the single most impactful MySQL performance setting on a dedicated database server.
questions.explain: innodb_buffer_pool_size controls the size of InnoDB's in-memory cache for table and index data. Because disk I/O is so much slower than memory access, this one setting typically has more impact on overall MySQL performance than any other configuration change.

questions.prompt: A table uses a randomly-generated UUID as its primary key and shows heavy fragmentation and slow inserts under load. Select every true statement about why, based on InnoDB's clustered primary key design.
options: InnoDB physically stores a table's data rows in primary key order inside the primary key's own B-tree, so a random key forces new rows into the middle of that structure repeatedly
Inserting into the middle of the clustered index's B-tree repeatedly causes page splits and fragmentation that a sequential, append-friendly key avoids
A sequential auto-increment primary key would let new rows append to the end of the clustered index efficiently instead
Secondary indexes in InnoDB store full table rows, not primary key values, so this problem only ever affects the primary key itself
This fragmentation problem is unique to MyISAM and doesn't apply to InnoDB tables at all
questions.explain: InnoDB's clustering means the primary key's B-tree is the table's actual data storage, so a random-order key like a UUID forces inserts into the middle of that structure repeatedly, causing page splits and fragmentation — exactly what a sequential, append-friendly key avoids. Secondary indexes actually store the primary key value alongside their own columns, not full rows, and this fragmentation problem is specifically a consequence of InnoDB's clustered design, not something unique to MyISAM.

questions.prompt: How does a transaction actually get "committed" under MySQL Group Replication, compared to traditional asynchronous source-replica replication?
options: The group runs a distributed certification process confirming the transaction doesn't conflict and that a majority of the group has durably received it, before any member considers it committed
The source commits locally first and returns to the client immediately, exactly as in asynchronous replication, then streams the change to the group afterward
Each group member independently decides when to apply the transaction, with no agreement protocol between members
A single designated member certifies every transaction alone, and the rest of the group simply trusts that member's decision without verification
questions.explain: Group Replication broadcasts a ready-to-commit transaction to the group and certifies it through a Paxos-derived consensus protocol (XCom), requiring majority agreement before any member treats it as committed — "get group agreement first," unlike asynchronous replication's "commit locally, then try to tell everyone else."

questions.prompt: Put these components of traditional MySQL source-replica replication in the order a single change actually travels through them, from being written on the source to being applied on the replica.
items: The source writes the change to its binary log (binlog)
The source's binlog dump thread streams the binlog event to the connected replica
The replica's I/O thread receives the event and writes it into the relay log
The replica's SQL thread reads the relay log and applies the event to the replica's data
questions.explain: A change starts in the source's binlog, is streamed out by the source's binlog dump thread, pulled in by the replica's I/O thread into its local relay log, and finally applied to the replica's actual data by the SQL thread — splitting the replica side into two threads is exactly what lets the I/O thread keep pulling even if applying falls behind.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a bootstrapped MySQL Router exposes classic-protocol port 6446, always routed to the current primary, and port ________, which load-balances read-only connections across the cluster's available read-only members.
questions.explain: Port 6447 is MySQL Router's default classic-protocol read-only port, round-robin load-balanced across available read-only members, while port 6446 always routes to whichever member is currently the cluster's read-write primary.

questions.prompt: A PostgreSQL backend process servicing one client's connection crashes with a segmentation fault. Per Lesson 58, what actually happens to the rest of the server as a result?
options: The postmaster detects the crashed backend and, as a safety measure, restarts the whole cluster into a clean state — isolation here is process-based, but a crash still triggers a full cluster restart, not a silent continue
Nothing at all — PostgreSQL is thread-based internally, so only that one thread terminates and every other connection continues completely unaffected
shared_buffers is permanently corrupted by the crash, requiring a restore from backup before the server can start again
The postmaster forks a replacement backend automatically and the client's session resumes exactly where it left off, with no interruption
questions.explain: PostgreSQL's isolation model is process-based, not thread-based, so a crashed backend doesn't directly corrupt its siblings' memory the way a shared worker-thread failure in theory could. But the lesson is specific that PostgreSQL still detects the crash and has the postmaster restart the entire cluster into a clean state as a safety measure — it's isolation plus a full restart, not isolation plus silent continuation.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of a real PostgreSQL install — whether by OS package manager or Docker's official image — per Lesson 59, in the correct order.
items: Install the PostgreSQL binaries, via package manager or by pulling the Docker image
Run initdb (often automatic) to create the data directory and system catalogs
Start the postmaster, which begins listening on its configured port
Set a real password for the postgres superuser account
Adjust pg_hba.conf to allow the real connections the deployment actually needs
questions.explain: Lesson 59 walks this as one logical sequence regardless of install method: binaries first, then initdb creates the cluster and default config files, then the postmaster starts listening, then the superuser password gets set before trusting any remote connection, and only then does pg_hba.conf get opened up deliberately for real traffic. Skipping straight to the last step without the earlier ones is exactly how 'PostgreSQL won't let me connect' support threads start.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about PostgreSQL's database/schema/tablespace hierarchy, per Lesson 61.
options: PostgreSQL connections are scoped to exactly one database; querying across two databases in the same connection requires an extension like postgres_fdw or dblink, not SQL Server-style three-part names
Every database starts with a default public schema, and objects inside it are addressed as schema.table
A tablespace is scoped to one specific database and can't be referenced by objects in any other database in the same cluster
Joining tables across two different schemas in the same database requires special cross-schema join syntax beyond ordinary SQL
search_path controls which schemas are checked, and in what order, when a query references an unqualified table name
questions.explain: PostgreSQL databases are genuinely isolated — no ordinary cross-database query, only an extension like postgres_fdw or dblink. Every database starts with a public schema, and schema.table is the addressing convention. A tablespace is actually a server-wide object, not scoped to one database — any database's objects can live in any tablespace the cluster knows about. And cross-schema joins in the same database use completely ordinary SQL, no special syntax, while search_path governs how unqualified names resolve.

questions.prompt: A SQL Server DBA new to PostgreSQL runs `CREATE USER app_user WITH PASSWORD '...';` expecting it to create something fundamentally different from a role. What actually happens, per Lesson 64?
options: CREATE USER is literally shorthand for CREATE ROLE ... WITH LOGIN — it creates exactly the same kind of object as CREATE ROLE, just with the LOGIN attribute already set
It creates a special 'user' object stored in a separate pg_users catalog, distinct from pg_roles
It creates a role with SUPERUSER privileges by default, since CREATE USER is reserved for administrative accounts
It fails, because PostgreSQL requires CREATE ROLE syntax explicitly and removed CREATE USER in modern versions
questions.explain: PostgreSQL has exactly one underlying concept, the role. CREATE USER is literal shorthand for CREATE ROLE ... WITH LOGIN — both create the same kind of object, and there's no separate 'user' system table; pg_roles is the one catalog for all of it, whether or not that role can log in.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: ordinary GRANT only affects objects that already exist. To automatically apply SELECT to every new table a migration role creates in a schema going forward, without re-running GRANT by hand each time, you'd use ________.
questions.explain: ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES is PostgreSQL's real answer to granting access to objects that don't exist yet — it sets privileges that get applied automatically to matching objects created after the statement runs, which ordinary GRANT, scoped only to existing objects, can't do.

questions.prompt: Match each pgAudit statement class to what it actually audits, per Lesson 67.
right: SELECT and COPY statements
INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, and TRUNCATE statements
CREATE, ALTER, and DROP statements
Role and privilege changes like GRANT, REVOKE, and CREATE ROLE
questions.explain: pgaudit.log accepts named classes of statements: read covers SELECT/COPY, write covers INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/TRUNCATE, ddl covers CREATE/ALTER/DROP, and role covers GRANT/REVOKE/CREATE ROLE and similar privilege changes — letting an org audit exactly the categories that matter for its compliance need instead of logging every statement indiscriminately.

questions.prompt: This dump is taken before a risky schema change. A week later, only the `orders` table needs to be restored into a different, already-existing database — not the entire dump. What does the `-Fc` format actually enable here, per Lesson 70?
options: pg_restore can selectively restore just the orders table from this custom-format archive, and can restore in parallel with -j — a plain -Fp SQL script can't be filtered this way at restore time
Nothing different from -Fp; both formats restore identically through psql -f
-Fc automatically splits the dump into one file per table on disk, the same thing -Fd does
-Fc captures only the schema, never the data, so a separate data-only dump would still be required
questions.explain: Custom format (-Fc) is a compressed, non-text archive built for pg_restore, which supports selective restore of individual tables or schemas and parallel restore with -j. A plain -Fp SQL script is just text replayed serially with psql — there's no way to tell it 'restore only the orders table' the way pg_restore allows against a custom-format dump.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about pg_basebackup, per Lesson 71.
options: It requires a role with the REPLICATION attribute and a pg_hba.conf entry that permits a replication connection
It reads data through ordinary SQL the same way pg_dump does, which is what makes its output portable across different PostgreSQL major versions
A base backup by itself is consistent only as of the moment it finished — restoring it alone doesn't let you recover to any later point in time
-X stream, the modern default, streams the WAL generated during the backup alongside it, making the backup self-contained
pg_basebackup can restore a single table on its own, without restoring the entire data directory
questions.explain: pg_basebackup rides the streaming replication protocol — the same prerequisites real streaming replication needs — not SQL, and the result is tied to the same major version and OS architecture it was taken from, not portable the way a pg_dump archive is. A base backup restores you to exactly the moment it finished, nothing more recent, unless combined with WAL archiving. -X stream makes the backup self-contained by capturing WAL generated during the backup itself. And it's a whole-cluster tool — no selective single-table restore without extra tooling.

questions.prompt: A pg_basebackup was taken at 1:00 AM. A bad DELETE with no WHERE clause ran at 9:14 AM. Put these point-in-time recovery steps, per Lesson 72, in the correct order to get the database back to 9:13 AM.
items: Restore the files from the 1:00 AM pg_basebackup into the data directory
Set restore_command so PostgreSQL knows how to fetch archived WAL segments back
Set recovery_target_time to 9:13 AM, just before the damaging DELETE
Start the server and let it replay WAL up to the target time, then stop there
questions.explain: Recovery starts from the physical base backup, then needs restore_command configured so PostgreSQL can pull back the WAL segments archive_command shipped out earlier, then recovery_target_time tells it exactly where to stop replaying, and only then does starting the server actually carry out that replay — landing the database one moment before the mistake, the same 'restore to right before it happened' shape as a SQL Server STOPAT recovery.

questions.prompt: Which statement accurately describes what VACUUM FULL does in PostgreSQL that plain VACUUM does not, per Lesson 77?
options: VACUUM FULL rewrites the entire table into a new file and returns the reclaimed space to the operating system, requiring an exclusive lock on the table for the duration; plain VACUUM only marks dead-tuple space as reusable inside the existing file, without shrinking it
VACUUM FULL only refreshes planner statistics, while plain VACUUM is the one that reclaims dead tuple space
VACUUM FULL runs automatically via the autovacuum daemon on a schedule, while plain VACUUM must always be triggered manually by a DBA
VACUUM FULL is a read-only diagnostic command that reports dead tuple counts without reclaiming any space at all
VACUUM FULL and plain VACUUM are functionally identical; FULL only changes how verbose the command's logging output is
VACUUM FULL reclaims space without taking any lock at all, while plain VACUUM is the one that requires an exclusive lock
questions.explain: Plain VACUUM reclaims dead-tuple space for reuse within the existing file but never shrinks the file or returns space to the OS. VACUUM FULL actually does return that space to the OS, but only by rewriting the whole table into a new file, which requires an exclusive lock for the entire operation — exactly why it's a deliberate, planned maintenance action rather than something run casually.
questions.distractorExplain: Option F reverses the actual locking behavior. Plain VACUUM is specifically designed to run concurrently with ordinary reads and writes, taking no exclusive lock on the table; VACUUM FULL is the one that requires an exclusive lock, since it's rewriting the entire table into a new file. Getting this backwards would lead a DBA to schedule VACUUM FULL casually during business hours, exactly when its real locking behavior makes that dangerous.

questions.code:
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT * FROM sales_fact WHERE region_id = 7;
-- Seq Scan on sales_fact (cost=0.00..820.00 rows=50 width=64)
--                        (actual time=0.02..41.10 rows=48000 loops=1)
questions.prompt: The plan line above shows an estimated rows=50 but an actual rows=48000 after running. What does this specific gap most directly suggest, per Lesson 75?
options: The table's statistics are stale or the planner's row estimate badly mispredicted this filter — a mismatch this large is frequently the real root cause behind a bad plan choice, and it's worth checking before anything else
The query is already optimally planned, since EXPLAIN ANALYZE always shows some unavoidable difference between estimate and actual by design
The table must be physically corrupted, since estimated and actual row counts are supposed to always match exactly
This kind of estimate-vs-actual gap only matters for JOIN operations, never for a plain Seq Scan with a WHERE clause
questions.explain: When actual rows is wildly different from the cost estimate's rows, the planner's statistics are stale or its estimate logic mispredicted the plan — and per Lesson 75, that mismatch is frequently the actual root cause behind a bad plan choice, more useful to notice first than the raw execution time.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: under PostgreSQL's MVCC model, an UPDATE or DELETE doesn't erase a row immediately — it leaves behind a ________, a row version no active transaction can see anymore that still physically occupies disk space until VACUUM reclaims it.
questions.explain: A dead tuple is a row version no active transaction can still see, left behind by UPDATE or DELETE under MVCC, continuing to occupy space until VACUUM marks it reusable — exactly the mechanism that lets a long-running transaction keep reading a consistent snapshot while other transactions change the same rows.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about shared_buffers, work_mem, and effective_cache_size, per Lesson 79.
options: work_mem applies per operation, not as one global budget — a single complex query can use several multiples of it at once across its sorts and hashes
effective_cache_size actually allocates additional memory for caching, on top of whatever shared_buffers already reserves
shared_buffers typically starts around 25% of system RAM rather than most of it, because PostgreSQL also relies heavily on the OS filesystem cache
Setting work_mem very high is always safe regardless of how many concurrent connections exist, since PostgreSQL caps it automatically server-wide
maintenance_work_mem is kept as a separate, usually larger budget specifically for operations like VACUUM and CREATE INDEX
questions.explain: work_mem is a per-operation allowance, not a single global cap, which is exactly why a complex query can claim several multiples of it at once. effective_cache_size allocates nothing — it's purely a planner hint about total cacheable memory. shared_buffers deliberately starts around 25% of RAM because PostgreSQL leans on the OS filesystem cache for the rest. work_mem has no automatic server-wide cap, which is precisely why setting it too high risks memory exhaustion under concurrent load. And maintenance_work_mem is its own separate, usually larger budget for VACUUM, CREATE INDEX, and similar maintenance work.

questions.prompt: A team wants a standby holding only three specific tables out of a 200-table database, kept continuously in sync. Per Lessons 80 and 82, which replication type fits, and why?
options: Logical replication, because a publication names specific tables rather than the entire cluster, while physical replication always ships WAL for the whole cluster with no concept of partial data
Physical replication, because streaming replication is always faster regardless of how much of the database is actually needed
Either type works identically here, since both replicate at the individual-table level by default
Neither — PostgreSQL has no way to replicate a subset of tables, so a nightly pg_dump of just those three tables is the only option
questions.explain: Physical streaming replication ships raw WAL and produces a byte-for-byte copy of the entire cluster — it structurally has no concept of 'some of the data.' Logical replication's publication/subscription model names specific tables, which is exactly why it, not physical replication, fits a request for only three tables kept continuously current.

questions.prompt: Match each physical streaming replication term to what it actually does, per Lesson 81.
right: Standby-side connection string pointing at the primary for streaming
Empty marker file whose presence tells PostgreSQL a data directory is a standby
Primary-side object that prevents WAL removal until its standby has consumed it
Standby mode that serves read-only queries while continuously replaying WAL
questions.explain: primary_conninfo is the standby-side setting pointing at the primary to open the streaming connection. standby.signal's mere presence, not its contents, tells PostgreSQL at startup that a data directory is a standby. A replication slot tracks how much WAL its standby has confirmed receiving so the primary won't recycle WAL that standby still needs. And hot standby lets a standby serve read-only queries while replay continues in the background.

questions.prompt: An application runs `SET search_path = app_schema;` right after connecting, then runs several queries over time. After switching to PgBouncer's transaction pooling mode, that search_path setting stops reliably applying to later queries. Per Lesson 83, why?
options: In transaction pooling, a server connection is returned to the pool as soon as one transaction ends, so a later query might land on a completely different backend that never ran that SET statement — session state isn't guaranteed to survive between transactions
PgBouncer silently blocks all SET statements in every pooling mode, so this would fail identically even under session pooling
Transaction pooling closes the client's own connection to PgBouncer after every transaction, forcing a full client reconnect and re-authentication
This is a PostgreSQL bug unrelated to connection pooling, fixed only by upgrading the PostgreSQL major version
questions.explain: Transaction pooling assigns a server connection only for the duration of a single transaction, then returns it to the pool immediately. The next transaction can be handed any available backend, including one that never ran the earlier SET search_path — which is exactly the session-state tradeoff transaction pooling makes in exchange for far better connection reuse under high-concurrency, short-transaction workloads.

questions.prompt: A migrated stored procedure includes `WHERE MiddleName = ''` to find customers with no middle name entered. Per Lesson 86, what actually happens when this runs against Oracle, and why?
options: It silently returns zero rows, because Oracle stores an inserted empty string as NULL for VARCHAR2/CHAR columns, and NULL never equals '' or anything else — the fix is WHERE MiddleName IS NULL
It returns exactly the expected rows, because Oracle treats '' identically to how SQL Server does
It raises a syntax error, because Oracle doesn't permit '' as a literal inside a WHERE clause
It returns every row in the table, because Oracle treats an empty-string comparison as always evaluating to true
questions.explain: Oracle treats an empty string as NULL for VARCHAR2 and CHAR columns, so a row with 'no middle name entered' actually stores NULL, not ''. Since NULL never equals anything, including another NULL, WHERE MiddleName = '' never matches those rows — the migrated code has to be rewritten to WHERE MiddleName IS NULL, exactly the kind of bug that passes testing on small data and fails quietly in production.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: unlike Oracle, which folds an unquoted identifier to uppercase, PostgreSQL folds an unquoted identifier to ________ — so CREATE TABLE Orders actually creates a table that must be referenced as orders, not Orders, per Lesson 87.
questions.explain: PostgreSQL's identifier folding runs in the opposite direction from Oracle's. An unquoted CREATE TABLE Orders creates a table genuinely named orders, and every unquoted reference resolves to that same lowercase name — the trouble starts only if a migration script quotes the identifier to 'preserve' the original casing, since quoting locks in exact-case matching for every future reference too.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about boolean representation across SQL Server, Oracle, MySQL, and PostgreSQL, per Lesson 89.
options: PostgreSQL is the only one of the four with a genuine native BOOLEAN type
MySQL's BOOLEAN/BOOL keywords are literally aliases for TINYINT(1), not a genuinely distinct type
SQL Server has a true native boolean type called BOOL, kept separate from its BIT type
Pre-23c Oracle has no native boolean column type at all, so a migration has to pick a convention like NUMBER(1) or CHAR(1) and apply it consistently
Oracle 23c's addition of a real BOOLEAN type means every Oracle database running in production today has native boolean support
questions.explain: PostgreSQL alone has a genuine native BOOLEAN among the four. MySQL's BOOLEAN/BOOL are just aliases for TINYINT(1). SQL Server has no true boolean type at all — it uses BIT, a 0/1 integer flag, for the same purpose, not a type called BOOL. Pre-23c Oracle likewise has no native boolean, forcing a NUMBER(1) or CHAR(1) convention. And Oracle 23c adding a real BOOLEAN type doesn't retroactively give every already-running Oracle database that feature, since a huge amount of Oracle in production predates 23c.

questions.prompt: Which statement accurately distinguishes the roles of AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) and the AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT) in a cross-platform migration, per Lesson 90?
options: DMS moves data — supporting both a one-time full load and ongoing change data capture — while SCT handles schema and code translation (procedures, functions, views); the two are commonly paired because neither covers the other's job
SCT moves the data, while DMS translates procedures and functions from the source dialect into the target dialect
DMS and SCT are two names for the exact same underlying tool, offered under different names depending on which AWS region a project is deployed in
DMS only supports migrations into Oracle, while SCT only supports migrations into PostgreSQL
SCT is Microsoft's tool for migrating into Azure, while DMS is AWS's equivalent — they belong to different cloud providers entirely
DMS handles schema conversion exclusively and has no data-movement capability of its own at all
questions.explain: DMS is the managed data-movement service, supporting a one-time full load and CDC-based ongoing replication for minimal-downtime cutovers. SCT is the separate tool that handles the schema and code translation — procedures, functions, views — that DMS itself doesn't do. They're commonly paired precisely because each covers a job the other doesn't.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B swaps the two tools' actual jobs. SCT is the schema- and code-translation tool; DMS is the data-movement service with full-load and CDC support. Reversing which tool does which would lead someone to reach for SCT expecting it to move rows, or for DMS expecting it to rewrite a stored procedure, and neither tool actually does that job.

questions.prompt: At Harborline, the FINAPP schema's objects live in a dedicated FIN_DATA tablespace rather than the default USERS tablespace. Per Lesson 92, what's the actual reason for that choice?
options: It keeps the finance schema's datafiles and growth separate from everything else in the instance, which matters for a system that closes the company's books and can't lose a transaction
Oracle requires every schema to have its own dedicated tablespace; the USERS tablespace can never hold application data
FIN_DATA is required specifically because the instance is named FINPRD, not for any storage-isolation reason
A dedicated tablespace is purely a licensing requirement attached to Oracle's financial application modules
questions.explain: The finance system is small in data volume but can't afford to lose a transaction, so Lesson 92 deliberately keeps FINAPP's tablespace separate from the default USERS tablespace — isolating its datafiles and growth from anything else sharing the instance, a storage-isolation decision tied to the system's actual reliability requirements, not an Oracle-wide rule or a licensing technicality.

questions.prompt: During a flash sale, checkout queries against storefront.orders slow down badly. Put these steps of diagnosing and fixing the MySQL incident, per Lesson 94, in the correct order.
items: Run EXPLAIN on the customer-lookup-by-email query and see type: ALL, a full table scan
Identify that there's no index on customer_email, so every lookup scans the whole orders table
Create an index on customer_email
Re-run EXPLAIN and confirm it now shows type: ref using the new index instead of type: ALL
questions.explain: Lesson 94 applies the same measure-identify-change-verify discipline to this incident: measure with EXPLAIN and see the full scan, identify the missing index as the cause, make the single targeted change of adding that index, then verify with EXPLAIN again that the plan actually switched from type: ALL to type: ref before declaring the fix done.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about where this course sits in the SQL Server Database Administrator path, per Lesson 96.
options: This course closes out the Multi-Platform Databases stage's first course, but not the stage itself and not the whole path
NoSQL, Document & Graph Databases is the course that actually completes the SQL Server Database Administrator path
The path's final stage pairs this course with a second course covering MongoDB, Cosmos DB, and Neo4j
This course and the next one are meant to make you equally deep in every platform covered, with no further specialization needed afterward
DP-300 marks the very end of the SQL Server Database Administrator path
questions.explain: This course closes its own place in the Multi-Platform Databases stage, but the stage and the path both continue into NoSQL, Document & Graph Databases, which is the course that actually finishes the path, pairing relational depth here with MongoDB, Cosmos DB, and Neo4j there. The path explicitly frames broad exposure as a checkpoint, not a finish line — deeper specialization is a deliberate later choice, not something this course or the next one hands you automatically. And DP-300 sits partway through the path, not at its end.
